units.greek: LIBER TERTIUS [3.pr.1] Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus. is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum. utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset! si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, qui, etiam si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur. igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare.

[3.1.1] Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent. ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur. proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum. namque non potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis, nisi uti hominis bene figurati membrorum habuerit exactam rationem. [3.1.2] Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, a medio pectore ad summum verticem quartae. ipsius autem oris altitudinis tertia est pars ab imo mento ad imas nares, nasum ab imis naribus ad finem mediûm superciliorum tantundem, ab ea fine ad imas radices capilli frons efficitur item tertiae partis. pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae. reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti.

[3.1.5] Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt. perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero est inventus. si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex X singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis. simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri.

[3.1.6] Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex. cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον ; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα .

[3.1.9] Ergo si convenit ex articulis hominis numerum inventum esse et ex membris separatis ad universam corporis speciem ratae partis commensus fieri responsum, relinquitur, ut suspiciamus eos, qui etiam aedes deorum inmortalium constituentes ita membra operum ordinaverunt, ut proportionibus et symmetriis separatae atque universae convenientes efficerentur eorum distributiones. [3.2.1] Aedium autem principia sunt, e quibus constat figurarum aspectus, ea: primum in antis, quod graece ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν dicitur, deinde prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros , hypaethros. horum exprimuntur formationes his rationibus. [3.2.2] In antis erit aedes, cum habebit in fronte antas parietum, qui cellam circumcludunt, et inter antas in medio columnas duas supraque fastigium symmetria ea conlocatum, quae in hoc libro fuerit perscripta. huius autem exemplar erit ad Tres Fortunas extribus quod est proxime portam Collinam.

term_table.greek_sentence: si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, qui, etiam si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For if it had been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen close at hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be tested not by uncertain judgements; rather, an outstanding and stable authority would be added to the learned and the knowledgeable, and the craftsmen themselves would win favour by their own expertise, who, even if they are not abundant in money, or have not acquired renown through the long standing of their workshops, or even through influence in the forum and eloquence, yet, when they are well prepared, could possess authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And to the learned and the knowledgeable an eminent and lasting authority would be added, and the artificers themselves would draw clients by their own expertise. Even if they were not abundant in money, nor had gained renown from the long standing of their workshops, nor even through favour in the forum and eloquence, they could, once they were prepared, hold authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.

term_table.greek_sentence: [3.1.1] Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent.
term_table.english_sentence_A: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects must grasp most diligently.
term_table.english_sentence_B: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects ought to hold to most diligently.

term_table.english_sentence_B: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects ought to hold to most diligently.

term_table.greek_sentence: ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur.
term_table.english_sentence_A: This, moreover, is begotten from proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία.
term_table.english_sentence_B: This, moreover, is produced by proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία.

term_table.greek_sentence: proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Proportion is the commensuration of a fixed part of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the system of symmetries is produced.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Proportion is the commodulation, by a fixed part, of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the principle of symmetries is brought about.

term_table.greek_sentence: [3.1.2] Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, a medio pectore ad summum verticem quartae.
term_table.english_sentence_A: [3.1.2] For nature has composed the body of a man in such a way that the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist-joint to the tip of the middle finger, is just as much; the head from the chin to the top of the crown an eighth; with the lowest part of the neck, from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown a fourth.
term_table.english_sentence_B: [3.1.2] For nature has so composed the body of a man that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, just as much; the head, from the chin to the top of the crown, an eighth; from the top of the chest, together with the base of the neck, to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown, a fourth.

term_table.greek_sentence: pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth.

term_table.greek_sentence: reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The remaining members too have their own proportions of measurement, and by employing these the ancient painters and famous sculptors obtained great and boundless praise.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The remaining members also have their own proportions of commensuration, by making use of which the ancient painters and noble sculptors also attained great and boundless praise.

term_table.english_sentence_A: [3.1.5] No less did they collect the systems of measures, which seem to be necessary in all works, from the members of the body—such as the digit, the palm, the foot, the cubit—and they distributed these into the perfect number, which the Greeks call τέλειον.

term_table.greek_sentence: si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex X singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And if in both palms ten have been made complete by nature from the joints, it was also Plato's view that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis (ten) is made complete out of ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες.
term_table.english_sentence_B: And if from the joints on both palms ten are completed by nature, it pleased Plato also that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis is completed from ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες.

term_table.greek_sentence: [3.1.6] Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex.
term_table.english_sentence_A: [3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing against this, said that the number which is called six is perfect for this reason, that this number has divisions agreeing in their ratios with the number six, thus: a sextans is one, a triens (trientes) two, a semis three, a bes, which they call δίμοιρον, four, a quintarius, which they call πεντάμοιρον, five, the perfect number six.
term_table.english_sentence_B: [3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing to the contrary, have said that the number called six is perfect, for this reason: that this number has divisions which, by their ratios, agree with the number six, thus: the sextans is one, the trientes two, the semis three, the bes, which they call dimoiros, four, the quintarius, which they call pentamoiros, five, the perfect six.

term_table.greek_sentence: cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον ; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα .
term_table.english_sentence_A: When it increases towards its doubling: with one as added above six, the ἔφεκτον; when eight has been made, which is a third added, the second tertiarius, which is called ἐπίτριτος; when, with a half added, nine has been made, the sesquialter, which is called ἡμιόλιος; with two parts added and ten made, the second bes, which they call ἐπιδίμοιρον; in the number eleven, because five have been added, the quintarius, which they call ἐπίπεμπτον; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, the διπλάσιον.
term_table.english_sentence_B: As it grows towards doubling, when an as is added above six, it is ephekton; when eight has been reached, because a third has been added, it is the second tertiarius, which is called epitritos; when nine has been reached by the addition of a half, it is the sesquialter, which is named hemiolios; when two parts have been added and ten has been made, it is the second bes, which they call epidimoiros; in the number eleven, because five have been added, it is the quintarius, which they call epipemptos; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, is diplasion.

A.translation: BOOK THREE [3.pr.1] Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, declared Socrates the wisest of all men. He, moreover, is recorded to have said, prudently and most learnedly, that the breasts of men ought to have been furnished with windows and open, so that they might hold their thoughts not hidden but laid open for examination. Would indeed that the nature of things, following his opinion, had established them unfolded and visible! For if it had been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen close at hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be tested not by uncertain judgements; rather, an outstanding and stable authority would be added to the learned and the knowledgeable, and the craftsmen themselves would win favour by their own expertise, who, even if they are not abundant in money, or have not acquired renown through the long standing of their workshops, or even through influence in the forum and eloquence, yet, when they are well prepared, could possess authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them. Therefore, since these matters have been established not thus, but as the nature of things has willed, it does not come about that men are able to judge, with talents obscured beneath the breast, how the sciences of the crafts, lying deeply hidden, really are.

[3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects must grasp most diligently. This, moreover, is begotten from proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία. Proportion is the commensuration of a fixed part of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the system of symmetries is produced. For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact system of members, as that of a well-shaped man. [3.1.2] For nature has composed the body of a man in such a way that the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist-joint to the tip of the middle finger, is just as much; the head from the chin to the top of the crown an eighth; with the lowest part of the neck, from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown a fourth. Of the height of the face itself, a third part is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the boundary between the eyebrows, is just as much; from that boundary to the lowest roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise a third part. The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth. The remaining members too have their own proportions of measurement, and by employing these the ancient painters and famous sculptors obtained great and boundless praise.

[3.1.5] No less did they collect the systems of measures, which seem to be necessary in all works, from the members of the body—such as the digit, the palm, the foot, the cubit—and they distributed these into the perfect number, which the Greeks call τέλειον. Now the ancients established as perfect the number which is called ten; for it was discovered from the number of the fingers of the hands. And if in both palms ten have been made complete by nature from the joints, it was also Plato's view that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis (ten) is made complete out of ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες. But as soon as eleven or twelve have been made, because they have gone beyond, they cannot be perfect until they arrive at a second decussis; for the single things are fractional parts of that number.

[3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing against this, said that the number which is called six is perfect for this reason, that this number has divisions agreeing in their ratios with the number six, thus: a sextans is one, a triens (trientes) two, a semis three, a bes, which they call δίμοιρον, four, a quintarius, which they call πεντάμοιρον, five, the perfect number six. When it increases towards its doubling: with one as added above six, the ἔφεκτον; when eight has been made, which is a third added, the second tertiarius, which is called ἐπίτριτος; when, with a half added, nine has been made, the sesquialter, which is called ἡμιόλιος; with two parts added and ten made, the second bes, which they call ἐπιδίμοιρον; in the number eleven, because five have been added, the quintarius, which they call ἐπίπεμπτον; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, the διπλάσιον.

[3.1.9] Therefore, if it is agreed that number was discovered from the joints of the human being, and that from the separate members there arises a correspondence of commensuration of a fixed part to the whole appearance of the body, it remains that we hold in admiration those who, in establishing the temples of the immortal gods as well, so ordered the members of their works that, by proportions and symmetries, their distributions were made to agree both as separate parts and as a whole. [3.2.1] The principles of temples, from which the appearance of their figures is constituted, are these: first the temple in antis, which in Greek is called naos en parastasin; then the prostyle, the amphiprostyle, the peripteral, the pseudodipteral, the dipteral, the hypaethral. The formations of these are expressed according to the following rules. [3.2.2] A temple will be in antis when it has on the front the antae of the walls which enclose the cella, and between the antae, in the middle, two columns, and above them a pediment placed with that symmetry which shall have been set out in this book. An example of this will be the one at the Three Fortunes, of the three (extribus) that which is nearest the Colline Gate.

B.translation: BOOK THREE [3.pr.1] The Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, declared Socrates the wisest of all men. He, moreover, is recorded to have said, prudently and most learnedly, that the breasts of men ought to have been windowed and open, so that they might hold their thoughts not hidden but laid open for examination. Would indeed that the nature of things, following his opinion, had made them unfolded and plainly visible! For had it been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen ready to hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be approved by no uncertain judgements. And to the learned and the knowledgeable an eminent and lasting authority would be added, and the artificers themselves would draw clients by their own expertise. Even if they were not abundant in money, nor had gained renown from the long standing of their workshops, nor even through favour in the forum and eloquence, they could, once they were prepared, hold authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them. Proportion is the commodulation, by a fixed part, of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the principle of symmetries is brought about. For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact relation of its members like that of a well-shaped man. [3.1.2] For nature has so composed the body of a man that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, just as much; the head, from the chin to the top of the crown, an eighth; from the top of the chest, together with the base of the neck, to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown, a fourth. The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth. The remaining members also have their own proportions of commensuration, by making use of which the ancient painters and noble sculptors also attained great and boundless praise.

Now the ancients established as perfect the number that is called ten; for it was found from the number of the fingers on the hands. But as soon as eleven or twelve are made, because they have gone beyond it, they cannot be perfect until they arrive at the second decussis; for the single things are small parts of that number.

The configurations of these are expressed according to the following principles. [3.2.2] A temple will be in antis when it has at the front the antae of the walls that enclose the cella, and between the antae, in the middle, two columns, and above them a pediment placed according to that symmetry which will have been set down in this book. An example of this will be at the Three Fortunes, the one of the three that is nearest the Colline Gate.
